rule: top-level `file.fun` (file basename); nested modules/functors dotted (`file.Make.connect`); local function lets `outer.f`, local value lets fold into the enclosing binding; module-level code's caller is the module. Code outside a method body: the caller is its location. Field/val initializer → `Type#field`; C# property accessor → `Type#Prop` (get) / `Type#Prop=` (set); Ruby setter → `Type#x=`; `static {}` block → `Type#<clinit>`. Non-lazy initializers also get an `implicit` edge from `<clinit>`/`<init>`; lazy ones do not.
spec_gap: What is the caller of a call inside a top-level non-function OCaml binding, `let default_path = load " /etc/app "` (line 3): the module `config` (module-level code, as for `let () = ...`), or `config.default_path` (a named binding, as Haskell top-level bindings are `Module.f` and field initializers are `Type#field`)? The same question applies to value lets inside a nested structure, `module M = struct let v = f () end` (`config.M` or `config.M.v`).
notes: The OCaml note decides top-level functions (`file.fun`), module-level code (caller = module) and local value lets (fold into the enclosing binding), but not a top-level non-function `let`. Line 1 (`String.trim`, caller `config.load`) and line 5 (`Stdlib.print_endline`, caller `config`) are clear; line 3 is not.
